blocks.text: A data-driven breakdown of execution microstructure, slippage math, and why algorithmic execution stops being optional the moment your size crosses $500K.

You spent months building the thesis. You nailed the macro, timed the entry, sized the position. Then you fired a market order and handed 15-20 basis points back to the order book in a third of a second.
At small size, that's a rounding error. At $1M+ on a thin perpetual like $HYPE, it's a recurring tax that compounds into seven figures a year.

Let me be upfront: I'm not an execution expert. What I am is curious — and willing to do the work. So I went and talked to whales who actually move serious size on @HyperliquidX , dug through the order-book mechanics, and pulled real execution data to understand where the money quietly leaks out. This article is the result of that research. A huge thank-you to @NitroOGFX  for sharing his real TreadFi execution data on large-size orders — the screenshots you'll see throughout this piece are genuine fills from a whale executing real size, not cherry-picked marketing numbers.

And here's the conclusion that research kept pointing to: if you're a big whale getting in and out of Hyperliquid positions, your realistic toolkit is @tread_fi , @InsilicoTrading, or native TWAP from @HyperliquidX or your own custom built execution engine, which not many has. So the real question isn't whether to use an execution tool. It's which one, and how much it's silently costing or saving you.

That's where @tread_fi  gets interesting — and it's worth knowing who built it. TreadFi was founded by @davidyjeong , who spent seven years as a Vice President in Quantitative Research at @MorganStanley Institutional Equity Division (MSET) — the desk responsible for the firm's algorithmic execution, transaction cost analysis, and execution consultation for institutional clients. In other words, the person who designed TreadFi's engine spent the better part of a decade building exactly this kind of infrastructure for one of the largest equity desks on Wall Street. The VWAP-tracking, participation-based, maker-first logic you're about to see isn't a crypto-native guess at institutional execution, it's the real thing, ported onto Hyperliquid.

This article shows you exactly how the execution tax is levied, precisely how much it costs (with real order-book math), and why a volume-participation engine like TreadFi's is the tool that recovers it. We'll benchmark all three options — TreadFi, Insilico, and HL's native TWAP — using that real whale execution data, not marketing claims.

One convention before we start, because it trips everyone up: negative slippage is good (you beat the benchmark — sold higher or bought lower than reference). Positive slippage means the market moved against you during execution. So when you see a +18 bps number later, don't panic — that's the market drifting, not the algo failing. We'll separate the two cleanly.
How Slippage Actually Works
Slippage isn't a vibe. It's arithmetic — and on a thin perp, it adds up fast.

A market buy doesn't fill at the top of the book. It sweeps through it, level by level, until you're full. Your price is the volume-weighted average of everything you ate. The thinner the book at each level, the more you pay walking up it.
So we pulled the live Hyperliquid book — HYPE and BTC, same timestamp, straight from the public API.
June 10, 2026, 10:18 UTC — api.hyperliquid.xyz/info, public, no key.
| | HYPE | BTC |
| Visible ask depth (API levels) | $1.25M | $40.4M (32× deeper) |
Now sweep a $1M market buy through the visible HYPE levels:
| Scenario | All-in cost (slippage + 4.5 bps taker) |
| Full visible book | 13.96 bps (~$1,396) |
| After discounting spoofed depth ($50K/level) | ~14.2 bps+ |
The same $1M on BTC, same moment: ~6 bps all-in — less than half the cost, into a book 32× deeper.

> (Depth, mids, and slippage are live, timestamped figures from Hyperliquid's public API — measured, not modeled. Note: the API returns the top 20 levels; the full native book carries more resting depth below that, so these figures reflect the visible top-of-book sweep. 13.96 bps on $1M = ~$1,396 — that's the bps cost in dollars.)

And there's a catch the raw number hides: a real chunk of visible depth is spoofed — resting orders that vanish the instant your sweep approaches. Once you discount each level to what's genuinely executable, your effective cost climbs above the optimistic ~14 bps. The book you see is the best case, never the expectation.
Depth is also volatile — minutes earlier HYPE showed just $237K in the visible levels. The top of book is a snapshot, not a promise.

Liquidity is the single biggest driver of your execution cost. HYPE slips ~2× harder than BTC on the same size, and spoofing makes your real fill worse than the screen suggests. On a book this thin, sweeping $1M as one market take is the most expensive way to do it. You want an engine that drips into real liquidity over time, not one that takes the spread all at once.
Get the Fees Right, or All Your Math Is Wrong
The entire maker-vs-taker argument hinges on fees, and this is where most analyses go wrong.
Hyperliquid base-tier perp fees:
Taker = 4.5 bps
Maker = 1.5 bps
That's a 3 bps swing on every single fill. On a $1M order, that's $300 of pure structural saving before slippage even enters the picture.

Three nuances whales should know: volume tiers cut fees (the highest maker tiers can earn rebates), HYPE staking unlocks additional discounts that stack on top, and builder codes add a small routing fee — which is why the TreadFi screenshots below show ~2.2 bps effective maker, still far below the 4.5 bps taker line.
The takeaway: every time an algo converts a taker fill into a maker fill, that's a 2.3-3.0 bps swing in your favor — guaranteed, before slippage.
VWAP — The Benchmark That Actually Matters

VWAP (Volume Weighted Average Price) is the average price weighted by what actually traded at each level. It's the yardstick every institutional desk lives and dies by, because it removes luck (arrival-price slippage just measures whether the market drifted your way), it measures your market impact, it defines fair value, and it's the universal compliance standard.
Beat VWAP and you didn't move the market against yourself. Miss it and you did.

This is where the VWAP-vs-TWAP distinction becomes the whole ballgame. A VWAP trajectory matches your pace to the market's real volume distribution — heavy window, trade more; thin window, wait. A TWAP trajectory ignores volume entirely and slices by the clock — fire a fat slice into a dead minute and you move price for no reason.
TreadFi is built to track VWAP — the exact metric the most sophisticated desks in the world are graded on.
The Real Execution Data
Theory is cheap. Here is real data pulled directly from TreadFi order screenshots on Hyperliquid.
Order 1 — $2M BTC Sell (Aggressive Maker VWAP)
Slippage: −5.327 bps (favorable) | VWAP slippage: 1.97 bps
100% Maker | 22.8% participation | 100% fill
Order 2 — $447K HYPE Buy
Slippage: −11.209 bps (bought cheaper than benchmark) | VWAP slippage: 1.678 bps
100% Maker | 100% fill
Order 3 — $1M HYPE Sell
Slippage: +18.712 bps (market drifted) | VWAP slippage: 5.319 bps
100% Maker | 100% fill

The key insight: across $447K, $1M, and $2M orders, TreadFi held VWAP slippage between 1.7 and 5.3 bps at 100% maker. A naive $1M HYPE market sell costs ~13-18 bps all-in. TreadFi executed at a fraction of that, repeatedly.

About that scary +18.7 bps on Order 3 — it's not the algo failing. Raw slippage swings with momentum; the market simply drifted during the window. The clean metric is VWAP slippage, which stripped out the drift and landed at just 5.3 bps. That's the entire point of benchmarking against VWAP: it isolates execution quality from market direction.
And critically — 100% maker means the fee sign swings in your favor. Instead of 4.5 bps taker, you pay ~2.2 bps effective maker. That's a 2.3-3.0 bps swing on every fill.
Insilico Terminal — A Genuinely Excellent Tool, With a Different Design Philosophy

Let me be clear upfront: @InsilicoTrading  is excellent. It's one of the most capable execution terminals available to non-institutional traders, and a lot of serious size runs through it for good reason. This isn't a takedown — it's a comparison of two well-built tools that make different design choices.
Insilico's order suite is genuinely sophisticated:

TWAP Chase — the flagship: time-sliced execution that posts maker-first per slice and falls back to taker only when needed. In liquid, range-bound conditions it will fill a large order largely as maker.
Chase orders — post at best bid/ask and continuously follow the quote until filled, with aggressive and patient modes.
Swarm orders — fragment a block into parallel orders to avoid sweeping the book in one shot.
Frequency jitter and irregular lots — real stealth features that make execution genuinely hard to detect on the tape.
This is real engineering. For a lot of order types and conditions, Insilico will execute beautifully.

The difference is philosophical, not a flaw. Based on Insilico's public documentation (as of mid-2026), its core order types are fundamentally clock-based: they answer the question "when should I try to fill?" — with a clock, plus jitter for stealth. They optimize timing. What they don't appear to do by default is size each slice to real-time market volume, or reference VWAP as the execution benchmark.

(If Insilico has shipped a volume-anchored or VWAP-benchmarked mode that isn't reflected in their docs, this distinction narrows — and I'd genuinely welcome the correction. But the screenshots below show what TreadFi delivers regardless of how that comparison shakes out.)

TreadFi makes the opposite primary choice. It optimizes quantity: it asks "how much is the market actually trading right now, and what's my fair share of it?" — and sizes into live volume against a VWAP benchmark. Insilico optimizes when to fill. TreadFi optimizes how much to fill relative to live flow.

For VWAP-benchmarked execution — the standard every institutional desk is graded on — anchoring to volume rather than the clock is the structural edge. Not because one tool is good and the other bad, but because volume-participation removes the one variable a clock can't control: what the market happens to be doing at the exact second your timer fires. That's the gap the next section makes concrete.
TreadFi Under the Hood
TreadFi separates trajectories (the math — VWAP, TWAP, Target Time, IS) from strategies (pre-configured bundles). Its Aggressive Maker config:
Trajectory: VWAP
Passiveness 0.02 → orders rest at top of book → explains the 100% fills
Discretion 0.08 → low wander, tight VWAP tracking → explains the 1.7-5 bps VWAP slippage
25% participation → slices sized to real-time market volume, not the clock
Passive Only → structurally maker, never crosses the spread

The tradeoff is honest: Aggressive Maker has no taker fallback, so in a fast breakout it may not complete on time. For that, TreadFi offers Impact Minimization — it keeps VWAP tracking but crosses to taker when falling behind, guaranteeing completion at variable cost. You pick the tool for the job.
Why Time-Based Is Luck and Volume-Based Is Structure

A clock-based algo fires every N seconds and cannot control what the market is doing at that exact second. Lucky: a big counterparty appears, thick book, great maker fill. Unlucky: a dead window, thin book, you force a market order into the worst liquidity. Over 20 slices, that's 20 coin flips — it averages near VWAP but with high variance, which makes execution cost unpredictable.

TreadFi's volume-participation engine asks a different question: "Is the market trading right now?" If yes, participate at 25% of that flow. If no, wait. The result: it never fires into a thin book, it automatically rides high-volume windows, there's no predictable pattern to front-run, and variance is structurally compressed — exactly why VWAP slippage stayed in the 1.7-5 bps band across every screenshot.

The adverse-selection honesty note: passive-only does have one real cost — you get filled preferentially right before the market moves against you. But VWAP tracking spreads you across the whole window so it largely washes out, the 3 bps fee edge buffers it, and in strongly trending markets you'd switch to Impact Minimization anyway. Passive-only is the right default in normal conditions; you switch when momentum is against you.
The Ideal Participation Rate

Rough intuition (a practitioner rule of thumb, not a hard law): if HYPE trades ~$10M per 15-min candle, then 5% participation is effectively invisible, 10-15% looks like a normal participant, 25% is noticeable, 50% means you are the market, and 75%+ is obvious and front-runnable. The classic optimal-execution framework (Almgren-Chriss) doesn't hand you a single number — it balances market impact against timing risk — but desks have long landed on ~10-15% as a practical sweet spot for most conditions.

TreadFi defaults to 25% — more aggressive than that heuristic — but because it's maker-only, a 25% passive participant impacts the book roughly like a 10-15% taker would. The maker-only nature offsets the higher target. Practical guidance: 10-20% on HYPE, 5-10% on BTC (the deeper book absorbs you easily), and tune it dynamically as conditions change.
The Full Cost Comparison
$1M HYPE order, by method (all-in: slippage + fees):
| Method | Cost | Basis |
| Market order | ~14-20 bps | measured — live book showed ~14 bps, worse with spoofing |
| Manual limits | ~10 bps + timing risk | maker fee, but telegraphs + adverse selection |
| HL Native TWAP | ≥4.5 bps fee floor + slippage + drift | always taker every slice |
| Insilico TWAP Chase | ~3-7 bps (est.) | maker-first + taker fallback |
| TreadFi Aggressive Maker | ~2-5 bps | measured — 1.7-5.3 bps VWAP slippage at 100% maker |

Savings vs. market order, by size: $20K saves ~$4 (skip it), $100K saves ~$60 (marginal), $500K saves ~$500, $1M saves ~$1,500. At $2M+, market-order cost scales non-linearly as you sweep deeper into the book — realistically a $5,000+ saving per clip, though the exact figure depends on book depth at execution time.

Annualized, for 5 × $1M HYPE trades/week: at a realistic ~18 bps for market orders versus TreadFi's measured ~3 bps, that's roughly $468K/yr vs. ~$78K/yr — a ~$390K annual gap on $1M clips alone. Scale the size or frequency and it runs into seven figures. That's not alpha. It's tax you're paying for no reason.
But What About Small Size?

Honest answer: at small size, algo execution is borderline. Below ~$100K, slippage is tiny and the 4.5 bps taker fee dominates, so TreadFi's value flips to mostly saving that fee (~2.3 bps) by going maker. But maker execution carries timing risk — the market can move against you while your limit waits. The net effect is small and can cut either way. Below $20K, just market order it. TreadFi's structural edge becomes decisive when slippage starts to dominate the fee — which only happens at size, which is exactly where whales live.
The Bottom Line

For the $500K–$5M range on Hyperliquid — the exact range in those screenshots — the case is closed by arithmetic. A naive $1M HYPE market order costs ~14-20 bps. TreadFi delivered 1.7-5.3 bps VWAP slippage at 100% maker, verified. Native TWAP is blunt, predictable, and always taker. Insilico is sophisticated but leaves quality to when the clock happens to fire. Volume participation removes that luck and compresses variance structurally — and the maker-vs-taker fee swing alone is a 3 bps edge on every fill (1.5 bps maker vs. 4.5 bps taker) before slippage even enters the equation.

And here's where it gets bigger than a single order book. At $5M+, no single venue can absorb you cleanly — you need to route across multiple exchanges, balance liquidity and margin in real time, and execute as one coordinated flow. Today that's the domain of in-house quant desks and OTC providers. That's exactly the layer TreadFi is building toward: one front door where you state your size, and the engine routes intelligently across venues, manages the liquidity, handles the margin — and you never have to think about where or how. The execution shown in this article is single-venue today. The vision is to make venue selection itself disappear. We're getting there.
Most traders spend months building a thesis and then donate 15-20 bps to the order book on execution. The thesis gets all the attention. The execution quietly determines whether you keep the edge.

At size, algorithmic execution isn't a luxury or an optimization. It's the minimum viable infrastructure. The fee is recovered on your first few trades. Everything after that is pure retention of the edge you worked to build.
The numbers don't care about your conviction. Price your execution, or the market will price it for you.
Built on real Hyperliquid order-book data, the verified HL fee schedule (4.5 bps taker / 1.5 bps maker base), and live TreadFi execution screenshots. Not financial advice.
